previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: James, a 60-year-old man with a history of alcohol use disorder, COPD, chronic pain, and hypertension, was admitted after presenting to the ED with alcohol intoxication, hypoxia, and cough. He was agitated and disoriented on arrival, with a high blood alcohol level and signs of possible early withdrawal. He received diazepam for withdrawal symptoms, along with oral thiamine, folic acid, and multivitamins. Despite medical recommendations to continue treatment for a suspected COPD exacerbation and incomplete pneumonia therapy, James refused further interventions, including nebulizers, physical exams, and ECG. He remained alert and oriented, with stable vitals, and chose to leave against medical advice. He was discharged home with instructions to resume his medications, stop drinking, and follow up with his primary care provider for ongoing management of COPD, hypertension, pain, and abnormal blood findings.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ year old male with alcohol intoxication, multiple admission 
for leaving AMA presenting with intoxication and hypotension.

# Alcohol Abuse/Dependence with Intoxication and Withdrawal: Has 
long history of alcohol use with repeated hospitalizations for 
intoxication. Has h/o DTs and seizures. Patient intoxicated and 
may be in early withdrawal given mild tremors but difficult to 
assess as patient is uncooperative.  His somnolence also likely 
a result of haldol. A section 35 was being pursued, however, the 
local courts were not open this AM due to the Veteran's Day 
holiday.  Patient started to become increasingly insistent that 
he leave, even though he agreed to stay for detox on admission.  
He was explained the risks of leaving against medical advice and 
understood these risks.  He shortly thereafter left the floor on 
his own.

leaving AMA, he had already left the hospital so I was unable to 
intervene. ***

dehydration from intoxication.  No signs of sepsis.

during previous admission and did not complete steroid and abx 
course. Here with cough and hypoxia but afebrile and without 
leukocytosis and thus unlikely pneumonia. CXR shows bibasilar 
infiltrates, but is more likely to be atelectasis.  He had 
gotten a dose of levofloxacin in the emergency department;
